questions.question: What is the cascade order for normal and important declarations?
questions.answer: Normal: user-agent < author. Important reverses priority: author !important is strong, but user !important outranks it for accessibility. Within the same origin, layers/specificity/source order decide.

questions.question: How is specificity calculated and compared?
questions.answer: As a tuple of (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements/pseudo-elements). Compare left to right; a single id beats any number of classes. Inline styles and !important sit outside the tuple.

questions.question: When is !important acceptable?
questions.answer: Only when you cannot change the competing rule: third-party/vendor CSS, email clients, or a deliberate utility escape hatch. If it is fighting your own code, fix specificity or use layers instead.

questions.question: Explain inherit, initial, unset, and revert.
questions.answer: inherit takes the parent's computed value. initial uses the property's spec initial value. unset inherits if the property is inheritable, otherwise initial. revert rolls back to the previous origin/layer.

questions.question: How do cascade layers change the winner?
questions.answer: Later declared layers beat earlier layers regardless of specificity inside them. Declare the order once, then fill layers. Unlayered normal styles generally beat layered normal styles.

questions.question: Rewrite a specificity war with layers so utilities always win.
Why can adding a class fail to override a style?
questions.answer: The existing rule may have higher specificity (id, more classes), be in a later layer, be inline, or use !important. Check the Styles pane to see the winning rule before adding more selectors.

questions.question: Why does margin not inherit to child elements?
questions.answer: Margin is not an inherited property; children start with their own initial margin (often 0 or UA default). Inheritance applies to properties like color, font, and line-height unless overridden.
